sections.title: 1. What Makes a Problem Interval DP?

blocks.text: Interval DP is the pattern for problems where the answer for a range depends on the answers for its smaller sub-ranges. You solve tiny intervals first and grow outward until you cover the whole array.
These problems often involve merging, removing, or combining elements, where the order of operations changes the cost.

blocks.caption: Solve the smallest intervals first, then combine them into larger ones

content.title: 1. What Makes a Problem Interval DP?

blocks.text: The tell-tale sign is a range of elements where the cost of solving the whole range depends on how you split it into two pieces, and the pieces interact when you combine them.
Classic examples are bursting balloons, merging stones, and matrix chain multiplication. In each, you decide the order in which to combine things, and different orders cost different amounts.

items: The state is a contiguous interval, written as i to j
Solving i to j needs the answers to smaller intervals inside it
You choose a split point and pay a cost to merge the two halves
The final answer is the whole interval, 0 to n minus 1

blocks.text: Define dp[i][j] as the best answer for the interval from i to j. To solve it, we try every split point k inside the interval, solve the left and right parts, and add the cost of combining them.

blocks.caption: Split the interval at k, solve both halves, then add the cost of merging

blocks.text: Because the two halves are smaller intervals, they are already solved. This is the essence of interval DP.

codes.python:
# dp[i][j] = best answer for interval i..j
for k in range(i, j):
    dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][j],
                   dp[i][k] + dp[k + 1][j] + cost_to_merge(i, k, j))

blocks.text: The trick that makes interval DP work is the loop order. We must solve shorter intervals before longer ones, because a long interval depends on the short ones inside it.
So the outer loop runs over the length of the interval, starting from the smallest. For each length we slide the interval across the array and try every split.

codes.python:
def solve(a):
    n = len(a)
    dp = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    for length in range(2, n + 1):                  # grow the interval length
        for i in range(0, n - length + 1):
            j = i + length - 1
            dp[i][j] = float('inf')
            for k in range(i, j):                   # try every split point
                dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][j],
                               dp[i][k] + dp[k + 1][j] + cost_to_merge(a, i, k, j))
    return dp[0][n - 1]

blocks.text:
The golden rule:

In interval DP, always iterate by increasing interval length. If you loop by i and j directly, you will read cells that have not been computed yet.
Once you know the shape, these all look familiar.

items: Burst Balloons: pick the last balloon to burst in each interval, not the first, so the neighbours are fixed.
Minimum Cost to Merge Stones: repeatedly merge adjacent piles at a cost.
Matrix Chain Multiplication: choose the multiplication order that minimises operations.
Palindrome Partitioning II style problems: some are interval DP over substrings.

blocks.text: Burst Balloons has a famous twist: it is far easier to think about which balloon is burst last in an interval, because then the two sides become independent sub-intervals.
When a problem is about combining or removing elements in a range, try this.

items: Confirm the state is an interval i to j whose answer depends on inner intervals.
Ask what it means to make the last decision (last split or last removal).
Write dp[i][j] as the best over all split points k of the two halves plus a merge cost.
Loop by interval length, smallest first, then by starting index, then by split point.
The answer is dp over the whole range, usually dp[0][n minus 1].

blocks.text: Interval DP is typically O(n cubed): two loops for the interval and one for the split point. That is expected and usually fine for the input sizes these problems use.
